name: Colin Kaepernick
role: American football quarterback (NFL 2011–2016) and civil-rights activist
summary: Kaepernick became a prominent activist after kneeling during the national anthem in 2016 to protest police brutality and racial inequality. He has since advocated the abolition of police and prisons, founded the Know Your Rights Camp, and supported Indigenous causes. He declined to vote in 2016, calling it support for a system of oppression, but later voted in 2020 and 2024 and in his 2026 memoir called that earlier choice irresponsible.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: His 2016 anthem protest was explicitly against a country that 'oppresses Black people and people of color'; he has since funded racial-justice organizations through Know Your Rights Camp, tied police abolition to ending anti-Blackness, and his July 4, 2020 post described Black Americans as having been 'dehumanized, brutalized, criminalized + terrorized'.

gradual-change.rationale: He describes policing and prisons as 'interlocking systems that are rotten to their core' and rejects incremental reforms as 'recycled' in favor of abolition, which implies disagreement with gradual change that respects established institutions. He has not spoken to the general principle directly.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: In 2017 he attended the Indigenous Peoples Sunrise Gathering on Alcatraz in solidarity, citing the occupation's aim to make the U.S. honor the Treaty of Fort Laramie, and said 'our fight is the same fight'. This suggests sympathy for Indigenous land claims, but he has not stated a position on Indigenous authority over traditional lands.

notes: His view of electoral participation changed: he refused to vote in 2016 ('the oppressor isn't going to allow you to vote your way out of your oppression') but voted for Biden and Harris and in his 2026 memoir called not voting irresponsible. This was not treated as evidence on democracy-best, which asks about forms of government. His 2016 shirt showing Malcolm X with Fidel Castro was also not used as evidence for any economic position. Most economic and foreign-policy statements have no recorded position.
